I'm glad you used the term 'marketable' here. It situates how important the temporal component is to all of this. It also allows us to analyze this in terms of a commodity. There is a distinct time pressure here, inside of larger cultural forces that were acting against the success of the Passion story. It's not as if Christ was a commodity that could be shelved while a few decades were allowed to pass until a long-haired teenager could dig Him him up from one of his dad's old crates of vinyls and bring Him back into fashion for a new age. If whatever the fire was which was sparked by the Christ story had not continued to grow during the time it did, wherein it relied on predominantly oral transmission through groups of Jews and pagan Greeks, Christ would have likely been forgotten or remembered faintly as some desert sage. But we know that this is not how he was remembered. It's retro-projected by some historians today in this fashion, but it just does not hold up to the earliest accounts.

The point I want to get across is that Christ wasn't something that people just casually kept around collecting dust on a shelf, like Beanie Babies, hoping someday the market might be right to go cash in. Moreover, it wasn't something that found itself preserved in a less mindful sense, like the baby blanket that gets lost behind the dryer and discovered centuries later at a time when it's conveniently marketable. It had to survive not being marketable at all, and what strikes us, is that despite the possibility for being much more marketable, the so-called creators of this story did not market it at all. And they appear to have died for the sake of not marketing something better.

The fact of the very early embarrassment of the crucifixion is critical. This was a case of a highly unmarketable idea surviving in a marketplace that was literally killing its early adherents. Some of the earliest disciples were killed in agonizing fashion. One might think that if you are being threatened with being boiled in oil, you might be inclined to testify with a story much grander than the one we in fact receive. "Yeah, I was there. He died on the cross and I saw Him come back down from the sky with doves, and it rained rose petals." Yet, what persists is the highly embarrassing story. That it would persevere in the Hebraic culture cannot be dismissed as a fluke or historical contingency. Take the Hebraic God holding in mind the nature of the Hebrew people. They formed some of the earliest complex economies. They're a highly practical, hierarchical and litigious society. They are obsessed with laws and lawful behavior. They tend to be a people that levy grievance, and have long historical memories, and grudges. In them, we get a revelation of a God that is highly litigious and highly punitive. In them we get the codified Laws of God. The God of the Jews is the God who gives us Law. A very behavioral orientation, and a very social orientation. How to express God in society.

This moves into the Greek where Stoicism and high art and architecture capture the virtue-turned-law of the Hebrews and transform it into a total system for world beauty. It achieves a new vision with the Greeks. A higher one. Naturally, because as a people they were far more high-flown than the Hebrews. Plato and Aristotle apply reasoning to God-seeking that the Hebrews never did, possibly never could.

They also experience God much more spatially and temporally than, say, the Hindus do. This is so very important.

The God of Christianity is always imminent. The apocalypse is coming. It's all situated in law and time. The individual is also highly important here.

With Hindus, the God experience is something different. It's far less about an explosion into the world around us with legal systems, economies, architecture. It's much more about turning the gaze of the mind inward on itself, a dissolving, and diffusion. The recognition of the trick and the falsehood of my own ego, and very importantly, that whatever God is, is in all of us. For the Hebrews and Greeks, God was external and Other. For Hindus, God is all, but it is within and we go inside, and it is us. There is a peace there, a quietness, a nothingness that we are after in order to experience God in this latter tradition. Where the Hebrews and the Greek minds are active, and we go through the motions of elaborate rituals and sacraments and prayer with a very material focus, with meditation, there is an altogether different praxis where we strip it all away, it's all bullshit keeping us from seeing what we are.

Importantly, there is the head room for mischief in Hinduism. For humor and for play in the divine, for the trickster. It isn't all Calvinist sinners in the hand of something angry.

I think the truth is bigger than we even think it is. Somehow these can both be true. There is a graveness in the sense that what we are can be annihilated based on how we live our lives.
